title: The Motorcycle Diaries
full_review:
In "The Motorcycle Diaries" (Focus), Gael Garcia Bernal plays 23-year-old Argentinian medical student and future Marxist icon Ernesto Guevara de la Serna -- known to history books as "Che" Guevara -- who, along with his best friend, sets out on an odyssey across South America in order to experience a world he had only known about in books.

Based largely on journals kept by Guevara during the eight-month, 8,000-mile trek and published posthumously under the same name, "The Motorcycle Diaries" presents audiences with a much kinder, gentler image of Guevara than that of the fiery revolutionary plastered on T-shirts and dorm room walls. As directed by Brazilian filmmaker Walter Salles, the film's idealizing tone will inevitably elicit strong opinions among both those who revere Guevara as a hero and those who vilify him as a monster.

Set in 1952, well before he became the bereted radical immortalized by photographer Alberto Korda's ubiquitous 1961 portrait, the film chronicles the continent-crossing road trip embarked on by Guevara -- the son of an upper-middle-class Argentine family, prone to crippling bouts of asthma -- and his Sancho Panza-like sidekick Alberto Granado (Rodrigo de la Serna), a biochemist and incorrigible womanizer.

Flush with a romantic spirit of adventure, they pile on Granado's beat-up 1939 Norton 500 motorcycle -- nicknamed "the Mighty One" -- and head off into the unknown.

Their travels take them from the frigid regions of Patagonia to the steamy jungles of the Amazon basin, making pit stops in Chile, Peru and Venezuela. Their journey becomes one of self-discovery, as they witness injustice and poverty among the indigenous mestizos, awakening in Guevara a sense of social conscience that would have a profound influence on his later leftist politics.

Though the film is beautifully crafted and at times quite moving, some viewers may find it difficult, given the hindsight of history, to reconcile the film's quixotic -- almost saintly -- portrayal of Guevara with the guerilla warrior of later years who advocated violence as a political tool and, less than a decade after the events depicted, helped establish a communist state in Cuba as Castro's right-hand man.

In tackling the complex and controversial role, Bernal ("Y Tu Mama Tambien" and Pedro Almodovar's upcoming "Bad Education") continues his rise to being one of the most exciting actors of his generation. His soulful eyes exude an inner blend of burgeoning conviction and innate self-doubt. Bernal's portrayal of the "Che" as sickly and sheepish stands in stark contrast to the more recognizable defiant machismo radiated by popular poster images.

The real stars in this film, however, are the downtrodden locals encountered along the way, many of whom are played by nonprofessional actors. The sweeping photography elevates the landscape from mere backdrop to being almost a character, capturing the continent's diverse topography from the snow-peaked Andes, to the sun-baked Atacama Desert.

What starts out as a conventional road movie gains emotional steam once Guevara arrives at the Catholic-run leper colony of San Pablo deep in the jungles of Peru. It is here, during a scene where he swims across a perilous river separating the medical staff from the afflicted residents, that Guevara's cinematic canonization from starry-eyed idealist to secular saint is completed.

Full of humanity and pathos, the film's treatment of religion -- namely Catholicism -- is a mixed bag of sensitivity and stereotype.

Taken for what it is, "The Motorcycle Diaries" is a poignant and inspirational call for social justice, reminding us of Guevara's words that "a true revolutionary is guided by great feelings of love." Unfortunately, by painting him in such morally heroic shades, the movie opens itself up to criticism by Guevara's own legacy, including his 1967 quote: "A people without hatred cannot vanquish a brutal enemy." This is a far cry from another revolutionary who preached an infinitely more radical message: Love your enemy.

Subtitles.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, some crass humor and recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
